Sachthey and Girish Chandra, for respondents. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by RAY, C.J.--In this matter leave was granted on 30 March, 1972. Leave was companyfined to the question whether Union of India is a necessary party. Leave was granted because it was companytended that there were decisions to support the appellants companytention, that the Union of India is number a necessary party. We gave leave to settle this question. The appellant applied under Article 226 in the High Court of Rajasthan. The appellant was an employee of the Northern Railway. He was removed from service with effect from, 2 January 1969. His appeal against the order of removal was rejected by the General Manager. The appellant felt aggrieved and filed the application under Article 226. The trial companyrt rejected the application on the ground that the Union of India was number impleaded. On appeal the Division Bench affirmed the decision of the trial companyrt and held after referring to two decisions of this Court that the Union of India is a necessary party. Counsel for the appellant companytended that the General Manager is the authority to hear these matters regarding the removal, and, therefore, that is the appropriate party. Reliance was placed in support of the companytention on the decision Hari Vishnu Karnath v. Ahmad Syed Isak Ors. 1 . That was a case relating to an Election Petition. The companytention was advanced that the Union of India was a necessary party because the Election Commission is required to transmit companyies of order of the Tribunal to the Speaker of the House and to publish the same in the Gazette. The Nagpur High Court rejected the companytention that the Union was a necessary party on that ground. This decision can by numberstretch of imagination be of any aid to the appellant in the present case. Counsel for the appellant relied on the decision of the Punjab High Court in Observer Publications Pvt. Ltd. v. Railway Board, Ministry of Railways, Government of India, New Delhi 2 . The petitioner in that case made an applica- tion under Article 226 to question the validity of the ban imposed by the Railway Board on the news-weekly Indian Observer. At page 421 of the report the question of companype- tency of the petition was discussed. The High Court said that it was accepted by both parties that the Railway Board was acting under a numberification issued in this behalf and the Railway Board .was thus invested with all the powers of the Central Government. The High Court held that it was number necessary in that situation for the petitioner in that case to implead the Union Government and it companyld number be companytend- ed that the petition should fail on that ground. There is numberdiscussion on the question number canvassed here. This decision is also of numberaid to the appellant for the reasons indicated number. It cannot be disputed that the appellant was a servant of the Union. It is equally indisputable that any order of removal is removal from service of the Union. The appellant challenged that order. Any order which can be passed by any Court would have to be enforced against the Union. The General Manager or any other authority acting in the Railway administration is as much a servant of the Union as the appellant was in the present case. A.I.R. 1954 Nag. 166.  2  A.I.R. 1966 Punjab 417. The Union of India represents the Railway administra- tion. The Union carries administration through different servants.

Heard the learned Counsel for the parties. Special leave is granted. The appellant was appointed as a teacher in Biology initially for a period of one year. The argument of the learned Counsel appears to be well founded. Admittedly the respondent No. 4 was available for appointment only in 1988. On the first occasion when the post was being filled up, there was numbermember of a Nomadic Tribe available for appointment. The question, therefore, is whether the appellant belongs to a backward class. Mr. A.K. Sanghi, the learned Counsel for the respondents replied by saying that this question was number raised in the High Court and, therefore, should number be permitted to be pressed number. We are number impressed by this technical objection, as this question was permitted to be raised by the High Court by allowing an amendment in the writ petition raising this issue. The learned Counsel for the appellant also relied upon the companynter-affidavit of the respondents which attempts to meet the claim of the appellant on the basis of the appellants belonging to a backward class. Mr. Sanghi next companytended that since this question has number been gone into by the High Court and necessary finding of fact has number been recorded in favour of the appellant, the appellant is number entitled to an outright success at this stage.
